claim: No published benchmark uses real production bot detectors (Cloudflare, DataDome, Kasada) as outsourced graders to score agentic browser tools on detectability — FP-Agent (2026) is the sole comparable work but uses the authors' own trained XGBoost classifier as judge, not live detectors, and is a one-shot study rather than a reusable harness.

votes.claim: No published benchmark uses real production bot detectors (Cloudflare, DataDome, Kasada) as outsourced graders to score agentic browser tools on detectability — FP-Agent (2026) is the sole comparable work but uses the authors' own trained XGBoost classifier as judge, not live detectors, and is a one-shot study rather than a reusable harness.
votes.reasoning:
The claim is a compound assertion. Its narrowest triple-intersection — (live edge detectors as graders) x (genuinely agentic/LLM browser tools) x (reusable harness) — does appear unoccupied by any single project I found. BUT two of the claim's specific factual sub-assertions are refuted by real, published work, which materially weakens it:

1. "Live production detectors as outsourced graders for detectability... in a reusable harness" is NOT novel/missing. Two published, reusable harnesses already do exactly this mechanism: techinz/browsers-benchmark (https://github.com/techinz/browsers-benchmark — Cloudflare, DataDome, Kasada, Akamai, Imperva, PerimeterX as LIVE graders, modular/extensible) and Ian Paterson's anti-detect-browser-bench (https://github.com/ianlpaterson/anti-detect-browser-bench — 31 live targets incl. Cloudflare/DataDome/F5, a 4-way ok/gated/blocked/error verdict classifier, 80 regression tests). Both grade against real deployed detectors, not a trained classifier. The ONLY thing separating them from the claim is that they score stealth/automation libraries (Patchright, Camoufox, nodriver, Playwright-stealth, etc.) rather than LLM-driven agents.

2. "FP-Agent is the SOLE comparable work" is false. Roundtable Research's "Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents" (https://research.roundtable.ai/bot-benchmarking/) explicitly scores LLM-based AI agents (alongside scripts and automation tools) against a mix of production detection systems (Cloudflare Turnstile, Google reCAPTCHA v3, hCaptcha passive, FingerprintJS Pro) plus their own Proof-of-Human. It is arguably MORE comparable to the described work than FP-Agent, since it uses (partly) live production detectors AND tests agentic tools. Its gaps vs. the claim: it omits DataDome/Kasada and the true edge-WAF bot-management stack, it leans on CAPTCHA/fingerprint vendors rather than the named edge detectors, and it is explicitly a one-off (code not yet released), not a reusable harness.

So: the precise niche the claim stakes out (named edge detectors x agentic tools x reusable harness) is genuinely open, but the claim overstates its own novelty — the "live-detector-as-grader reusable harness" pattern is already established (just on stealth libs), and FP-Agent is not the sole comparable work (Roundtable is a closer comparable on the agentic axis). No single project cleanly refutes the fully-qualified claim, so I cannot call it refuted; but the supporting framing is demonstrably wrong, so I cannot call it confirmed. Hence uncertain. Recommendation: rewrite the angle to (a) cite browsers-benchmark / ianlpaterson as prior art for the harness mechanism and Roundtable for AI-agent grading, and (b) position the contribution precisely as 'first reusable harness applying the named edge-WAF detectors as graders to LLM-driven agentic browser tools', which is the only defensible gap.

votes.reasoning: The FP-Agent sub-claim is accurate (own XGBoost judge; "first controlled measurement study"; live Cloudflare only in a limited case study). But the central assertion that no benchmark uses live production detectors as graders and that FP-Agent is the "sole comparable work" is contradicted by at least three published, reusable harnesses that implement exactly that methodology: techinz/browsers-benchmark (live Cloudflare/DataDome/Kasada/Akamai as graders, MIT, reusable), Ian Paterson's anti-detect-browser-bench (31 Cloudflare targets, 651 OK/gated/blocked verdicts, reusable, 80 tests), and browser-use's Stealth Bench V1 (71 tasks evaluating stealth across anti-bot protections, reusable, scoring the agent-infrastructure stack). FP-Agent is in fact the LEAST methodologically comparable of these, since it is the only one NOT using live detectors as the grader. The asserted novelty — "live detectors as outsourced graders + reusable harness, unlike FP-Agent's classifier" — is therefore well-established prior art, not a gap. The entire remaining gap rests on a single undeveloped qualifier, "agentic/LLM-driven" vs "browser automation engine / stealth tool / infra provider." That qualifier has a real but narrow kernel (per FP-Agent's own finding, the LLM-driven behavioral layer, not the engine fingerprint, is what distinguishes agents, and engine/stealth benchmarks grade mostly IP/TLS/fingerprint), yet agentic tools inherit those engine fingerprints and browser-use's bench already scores the provider stack agents run on. So the gap as worded is largely an artifact of too-narrow definition: an adjacent tool already covers the methodological core, and the claim misidentifies its closest prior art. A defensible residual exists (live-detector grading of the LLM behavioral layer during task execution), but it is far narrower than the claim states and is not what the wording protects — hence refuted as stated, with a recommendation to reframe around the behavioral-execution residual rather than the false "no live-detector harness exists" framing.

votes.claim: BrowserGym occupies the multi-tool-adapter slot for task-success benchmarks but leaves the detectability and security axes entirely open; no multi-tool harness exists that compares Playwright, browser-use, Stagehand, Skyvern, Feather, and nodriver on how detectable or exploitable they are.
votes.reasoning:
The claim's narrow framing (the EXACT 6-tool union — including the author's own private "Feather" — scored on BOTH detectability AND exploitability in one harness) genuinely does not exist verbatim. But the claim as written makes two strong, falsifiable assertions that the evidence contradicts:

1. "Leaves the detectability axis entirely open / no multi-tool harness exists that compares [these tools] on how detectable they are." This is false. There are at least TWO public multi-tool detectability harnesses that overlap the named tool set:
- FP-Agent (arXiv 2605.01247, May 2026) is a reusable, fully open-sourced (GitHub + dataset) measurement harness that fingerprints SEVEN agentic browsing agents — including Browser Use and Skyvern (2 of the 6 named tools) — on browser + behavioral fingerprints, with a honey-site instrumentation pipeline and a classifier that detected all 7 agents where Cloudflare detected only 1. This is precisely "a multi-tool harness comparing agentic browser tools on how detectable they are."
- Ian Paterson's "Anti-detect browser benchmark 2026" runs 7 stealth frameworks — including nodriver and vanilla Playwright (2 more of the 6 named tools), plus Patchright, Camoufox, rebrowser — across 31 Cloudflare/anti-bot targets (651 verdicts), explicitly measuring "how the browser is being driven." That is a multi-tool detectability harness covering the nodriver/Playwright slice.
Between them, 4 of the 6 specifically-named tools (Browser Use, Skyvern, nodriver, Playwright) are already compared on detectability by existing public harnesses. The axis is not "entirely open."

2. "Leaves the security axis entirely open." Also false. WASP (web-agent security vs prompt injection), AgentDojo (NeurIPS 2024; 97 tasks / 629 security cases), BrowseSafe-Bench, and VPI-Bench are public multi-agent security/exploitability benchmarks; published evaluations explicitly test Browser Use and Agent-E susceptibility to prompt injection.

Where the claim retains a kernel of truth: the existing harnesses are siloed — FP-Agent covers agentic tools but not nodriver/Playwright/Stagehand; Paterson covers stealth libs but not the agentic frameworks; security benchmarks are model/agent-centric rather than browser-driver-detectability-centric. No single harness unifies stealth libraries + agentic frameworks + Feather across both detectability AND exploitability. So Feather's tower targets a real, under-served INTERSECTION. But the claim does not say "no unified harness across both axes" — it says the axes are "entirely open" and "no multi-tool harness exists" on detectability/exploitability, and that strong form is refuted by FP-Agent (detectability, overlapping Browser Use + Skyvern) and the anti-detect benchmark (detectability, overlapping nodriver + Playwright). Recommend the research angle be reworded to claim the unified/cross-axis niche, not an empty axis.

votes.reasoning:
The gap is REAL but the claim's wording overstates it; "entirely open" is wrong, and the honest, defensible version is narrower than stated.

What the research actually shows — the benchmark landscape splits cleanly into two non-overlapping worlds:

1. TASK-SUCCESS world: BrowserGym (unified Gymnasium API wrapping WorkArena/WebArena/etc.), WebVoyager, Skyvern's Web-Bench. These score agentic tools (browser-use 89.1%, Skyvern 85.8%) on task completion only. BrowserGym is more precisely a multi-BENCHMARK adapter than a multi-TOOL adapter (agents plug into it), but the claim's framing of its slot is essentially right.

2. DETECTABILITY world: mature multi-tool benches already exist — techinz/browsers-benchmark and ianlpaterson's anti-detect benchmark (651 verdicts, 7 tools, 31 Cloudflare targets). Critically, these test LOW-LEVEL DRIVERS / anti-detect engines (Playwright, nodriver, Camoufox, Patchright, Selenium, ZenDriver) and EXCLUDE the agentic LLM tools (browser-use, Stagehand, Skyvern absent), and measure only bot-detection bypass — no exploitability.

3. EXPLOITABILITY/SECURITY world: actively researched but separate — ST-WebAgentBench, VPI-Bench (visual prompt injection for computer-use agents), AgentDyn, and in-browser LLM-guided prompt-injection fuzzing harnesses. These target agent/LLM safety, not a cross-tool detectability scoreboard.

Where the claim is RIGHT (the non-trivial real gap): No single harness puts BOTH the driver-level tools AND the agentic tools on the same bench and scores detectability AND exploitability together. The two halves of the named tool list live in two disconnected benchmark cultures; neither crosses into the other's tool set or measures both axes. That synthesis — agentic-behavioral detectability (does the agent's reasoning/timing/navigation loop emit signals beyond the underlying driver's fingerprint?) plus a comparative per-tool exploitability scoreboard — is genuine white space.

Where the claim OVERSTATES (skeptic's caveats, but not fatal):
- "Entirely open" is false for detectability — it is well-covered for the driver subset.
- Part of the agentic-tool detectability axis is DERIVABLE from existing driver benches: Stagehand runs on Patchright (already in techinz's bench) and browser-use runs on Playwright/patchright, so their network/fingerprint detectability ~ approximates their backend's. This is the strongest refutation angle and it dents the novelty of the detectability half.
- Including Feather (the author's own unpublished tool) in the tool list makes the literal "no harness compares [these exact 6]" tautologically true and slightly self-serving.

Net: strip the rhetorical "entirely" and the self-referential Feather, and a substantive, non-trivial gap survives — a unified cross-category (driver + agentic), cross-axis (detectable + exploitable) bench does not exist, and the agentic-behavioral and comparative-exploitability portions are not derivable from current work. That is a meaningful methodological position, not an artifact of over-narrow definition. Verdict: confirmed, with the explicit honesty that "entirely open" is an overstatement and the detectability axis is partly pre-covered for the driver subset.

votes.reasoning: The claim conflates two separable things, and research splits them. REFUTED part: "authenticated agent evaluation is unoccupied" and "TheAgentCompany is the closest precedent" are both wrong. WebBench (Halluminate/Skyvern) is a published, leaderboard-backed benchmark evaluating browser agents on ~2,454-5,750 tasks across 452 LIVE real-world top-1000 websites, explicitly including login, 2FA, and credential-guarded portals; the authors created real accounts and supplied credentials, and Skyvern reports SOTA 64.4%. That is a real-world authenticated agent evaluation and is far closer to the target than TheAgentCompany's synthetic internal tools. WorkArena/WorkArena++ (ServiceNow, ~20k+682 instances) and WebSP-Eval (real accounts + persistent state across runs on 28 sites) further occupy the authenticated space. So the framing assertions are demonstrably false. SURVIVING kernel: the SPECIFIC "Cookie Mine" condition — an agent RIDING a pre-warmed HUMAN persistent-cookie session (trust accrued by real human browsing) with STEALTH/detectability scored alongside task success — does appear to lack a published baseline. WebBench has the agent log in itself with fresh credentials and does not measure stealth; the stealth axis exists separately (browser-use stealth benchmark, headless vs headful detection) but is decoupled from authenticated task success. No single benchmark found combining warmed-human-cookie sessions + stealth + value. Verdict is uncertain rather than confirmed because the claim's load-bearing assertions are refuted by WebBench, and only a narrowly-reworded version (drop "unoccupied"/"TheAgentCompany closest precedent"; scope the gap to the stealth + human-warmed-cookie combination) holds. Recommend the researcher tighten the claim accordingly.

votes.claim: Authenticated/warmed-session agent evaluation is unoccupied: TheAgentCompany is the closest precedent (agents log into synthetic internal tools), but no benchmark evaluates agents driving real-world persistent-cookie sessions (the Cookie Mine model), so the highest-stealth, highest-value use case has no published eval baseline.

votes.reasoning:
The gap survives a deliberate hunt for a refuting benchmark; the adjacent tools each cover a different slice, and none isolates the warmed-real-session variable.

WHAT THE CLAIM GETS RIGHT (verified against primary/vendor sources):
- TheAgentCompany framing is accurate. It is a self-hosted SYNTHETIC software company (GitLab, Plane, ownCloud, RocketChat) where agents are PRE-authenticated. Synthetic + pre-authed, not real-world persistent human cookies. It is genuinely the closest "authenticated agents" precedent.
- The mainstream web-agent benchmark corpus does not occupy the warmed-real-session cell, each for a different reason: WebVoyager EXPLICITLY omits login/CAPTCHA sites; WebArena/WebChoreArena/BrowserGym use self-hosted synthetic sites; Online-Mind2Web tests live sites but does not center authenticated/warmed sessions; ST-WebAgentBench/WebSP-Eval cover safety/privacy, not warmed-session stealth.

WHY ADJACENT TOOLS DON'T CLOSE IT (the key skeptic test):
- Web Bench (Skyvern) DOES test login on real portals, but the agent authenticates FRESH from stored credentials, and bot-detection is logged as an infrastructure failure CATEGORY — not the studied variable. Cold login is the opposite of riding a pre-warmed human session.
- BrowserBench (Halluminate) and Roundtable's bot-detection benchmark DO measure stealth/"Stealth Failure Rate", but both are SILENT on session warmth and run on fresh agent sessions; neither varies human-session warmth as an independent variable.
- Browser Use's cookie-syncing / real-Chrome-profile export is a PRODUCT feature, not an eval — its existence without a published baseline actually supports the claim.

THE DECISIVE FINDING: "Warmed session" / "account warming" lives almost entirely in gray-market anti-detect-browser tooling (Undetectable.io, GeeLark, Nextbrowser, anti-detect vendors). Their evidence is uncontrolled marketing self-claims ("In tests, warmed profiles consistently perform better than fresh ones") — exactly a published eval baseline does NOT exist. So the variable is commercially significant yet academically un-benchmarked: two communities (web-agent benchmarkers; bot-detection researchers) each touch an adjacent edge, neither holds warmed-real-human-session as the controlled variable measuring its task-success/stealth effect.

WHY NOT TRIVIAL/OVER-NARROW: It is not one cherry-picked site or task — it is a whole experimental axis (real persistent human trust context as a stealth/value lever) with a real commercial footprint but no reproducible baseline. That is a non-trivial methodological gap, not a definitional artifact.

CAVEATS lowering certainty short of "ironclad": (1) The components all exist separately, so a critic could call the gap "merely uncombined" rather than conceptually novel — but uncombined-with-no-baseline is still a real eval gap. (2) The superlative "highest-stealth, highest-VALUE use case" is an editorial assertion I could not independently benchmark; the defensible, verified core is narrower: no published eval baseline isolates agents driving warmed real-world persistent-cookie sessions. With that scoping, the gap is real and non-trivial.

The claim has a real kernel but materially overstates differentiation in three ways, so as worded it is overclaimed.

TheAgentCompany is a SELF-HOSTED SYNTHETIC environment (GitLab/OwnCloud/Plane/RocketChat), so its logins are not real-world persistent-cookie sessions — it is a fairly DISTANT precedent. Multiple sources note academic benchmarks deliberately EXCLUDE login/real authenticated sessions for ethical/legal reasons (can't share real accounts/recorded auth traces; warmed-human-cookie stealth borders ban-evasion). So the niche is under-served partly because publishing it as a benchmark is ethically fraught — not purely because it is untapped high-value-and-hard. The claim presents an ethics-driven avoidance as a pure greenfield opportunity.

Net: the precise "warmed-human-session-as-stealth-vector" benchmark does appear unpublished (real kernel), but the claim overstates the differentiation by naming a distant precedent while missing nearer ones, by framing two already-occupied axes as a single empty niche, and by asserting "highest-value" while ignoring the ethical reason the space is avoided. The differentiation is overstated: the field is well-occupied by adjacent multi-tool stealth harnesses, the named "closest work" is mischaracterized (it HAS a common-adapter harness), and the truly-closest open-source agentic-layer harness is omitted.

1) Benchmarks exclude auth. The browser-use stealth benchmark explicitly states its task design is "No auth" and failure only means "the browser got blocked" on anonymous challenge pages (Cloudflare/Datadome/PerimeterX targets). Roundtable's "Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents" tests five ANONYMOUS form scenarios (signup, survey, review, article-unlock, psych experiment) with "no pre-existing account state." The anti-detect benchmark genre (ianlpaterson's 7-tool/31-Cloudflare-target run, CloakBrowser's 30/30, GoLogin/Multilogin reviews) scores fingerprint consistency and Cloudflare/CAPTCHA bypass, not in-session authenticated detectability. The FP-Inconsistent academic study (Vekaria et al., IMC 2025) measures fingerprint-evasion against commercial anti-bots, again unauthenticated.

2) HUMAN Security's 2026 State of AI Traffic report DOES document agentic traffic inside logged-in sessions at measurable scale: account pages 8.82% and authentication flows 4.95% of agentic traffic, with explicit language that "agents are operating within logged-in sessions on behalf of users" and completing authenticated checkout flows. So the real-world phenomenon is verified.

3) Gap coverage. I tried the most plausible refutations: anti-detect browsers (Multilogin/GoLogin) operate in authenticated multi-account contexts but publish NO detectability benchmark with methodology — only "no bans" marketing and fingerprint tests; behavioral-biometrics / ATO vendors (BioCatch-style, Sardine, GeeTest) DO detect automation inside authenticated sessions in production, but that is a detector capability, not a public stealth-comparison eval of agentic tools; academic hits (Risk-Based Authentication empirical study, ST-WebAgentBench safety benchmark, fake-account/Sybil detection) address adjacent problems, none is a warmed-session stealth detectability eval.

Residual caveat (why not a stronger "verified law"): the absolute "zero existing coverage" is true on the eval/benchmark axis I could survey publicly, but in-session automation detection clearly EXISTS as a commercial capability — it simply is not packaged as an open stealth/detectability benchmark. So the gap is specifically a benchmark/eval gap, not a "nobody can detect this" gap. With that framing, the claim stands. No competitor project occupies the warmed-authenticated-session detectability-eval slot — which is exactly Feather's Cookie-Mine/tower territory.

votes.reasoning:
The core gap is methodologically real and non-trivial, though the claim's absolutist wording overstates on two points.

GAP IS REAL: The canonical stealth benchmarks (CreepJS, Sannysoft, Rebrowser bot-detector, BrowserScan, Pixelscan, fingerprint.com, DataDome/incolumitas bot test) all operate at the anonymous fingerprint / automation-artifact layer (canvas, WebGL, audio, navigator props, signal-consistency lie-detection) served from a cold-session probe page. None evaluate a warmed/logged-in session. This is a genuinely different detection regime: a tool can score 100% on CreepJS yet be trivially caught inside a warmed account via velocity, behavioral anomaly, account-graph, and post-login reputation signals. So a fingerprint benchmark yields a MISLEADING detectability score for the actual deployment context of warmed agentic automation — a substantive methodological blind spot, not a hair-splitting niche. HUMAN Security's 2026 report independently verifies the second leg: agents 'operate within authenticated sessions,' complete checkouts and manage accounts; post-login account compromise quadrupled (~402k/org, 2025); agentic traffic grew 7,851% YoY; agentic browsers ~73% of agentic traffic. The gap therefore tracks the highest-value, fastest-growing threat surface — the opposite of a contrived definition. No adjacent stealth-benchmark / comparison project covers this layer.

WHERE THE CLAIM OVERSTATES (caveats, not refutation): (1) 'explicitly excludes' is wrong — benchmarks don't state an exclusion; authenticated sessions are out of scope by construction because a generic reproducible public probe cannot require a site-specific warmed cookie. It's implicit non-coverage driven by methodological tractability, not oversight. (2) 'zero existing coverage' is true only in the narrow, correct reading (open stealth-side detectability benchmarks). It is FALSE if read broadly: authenticated-session bot DETECTION is a mature industry — behavioral-biometrics/ATO vendors (BioCatch, Sardine, DataDome account protection, GeeTest, CrossClassify) run inside logged-in sessions in production with comparative accuracy tests (e.g., 87% vs reCAPTCHA 69%). What is absent is an OPEN stealth-comparison benchmark for that layer, not all coverage of bots-in-authenticated-sessions.

VERDICT: confirmed on the substance — within the claim's own stated category ('bot-detection benchmarks, detector aggregators & stealth-comparison projects') the gap is real, meaningful, and uncovered by any adjacent benchmark. Recommend tightening the language to 'no open stealth benchmark covers the authenticated-session layer (the detection side covers it only via proprietary ATO products)' rather than 'explicitly excludes' / 'zero existing coverage'.

The substantive gap holds up under primary-source checking, though two absolutist phrasings are loose and should be tightened before the claim is leaned on.

WHAT VERIFIED CLEANLY:
1. The HUMAN Security 2026 driver is real and quantified. The "2026 State of AI Traffic & Cyberthreat Benchmark Report" documents agentic traffic inside logged-in sessions at measurable scale: account pages = 8.82% of agentic traffic, authentication flows = 4.95%, checkout = 2.31%; retail leads at 46.6%. The report explicitly recommends moving "beyond static identity-based controls toward continuous behavioral validation across the entire session lifecycle." That last line is the load-bearing point: the detection industry itself names session-lifecycle behavioral signals as the live frontier.
2. The existing stealth benchmarks do NOT cover this. CreepJS, BrowserScan, rebrowser-bot-detector, sannysoft, pixelscan, IPhey are stateless fingerprint / automation-leak probes (canvas/WebGL/audio/navigator.webdriver/Runtime.enable CDP leaks). I confirmed via the WebScraping Club "Anti-Detect Browser Royal Rumble" that even purpose-built anti-detect-browser benchmarks score only CreepJS + BrowserScan trust scores and that "login state plays zero role." The mainstream web-agent benchmarks (GAIA, OSWorld, WebArena, Tau²-Bench, METR) score task success / policy / safety — not detectability at all. So no public benchmark scores an agent's detectability while it rides a warmed, authenticated session via behavioral/session-lifecycle signals. That specific eval cell is genuinely unoccupied.

WHY IT IS UNDER-SERVED (valuable-and-hard, not low-value): occupying it requires real warmed accounts on real authenticated sites plus behavioral-fidelity scoring over a session lifecycle — it cannot be a stateless probe page, and it carries ToS/ethics friction. That difficulty explains the absence; it is not absent for lack of value (HUMAN's own data + pivot recommendation make it the frontier).

WHERE THE CLAIM OVERSTATES (caveats, not refutations):
- "explicitly excludes" overstates. The benchmarks don't deliberate over authenticated sessions and reject them; they are simply stateless/orthogonal — session state is out of architectural scope, not an announced exclusion. Reframe to "are stateless and don't model session state at all."
- "zero existing coverage" is true only for the precise behavioral-detectability eval. The warmed-session SUBSTRATE is a crowded commercial space — anti-detect browsers (Multilogin, GoLogin, AdsPower, Kameleo) are an entire industry built on persistent profiles + cookie/localStorage persistence, and they ARE benchmarked (on fingerprint only). A reviewer can say "warmed sessions are benchmarked all the time," which blunts a naive reading. The defensible framing is narrower and stronger: "no public benchmark scores agent DETECTABILITY via SESSION-LIFECYCLE BEHAVIORAL signals inside warmed authenticated sessions — the exact vector HUMAN says detectors are pivoting to."

NET: real, valuable, hard, and genuinely unoccupied as an eval — worth occupying — so confirmed. But tighten the two absolutist phrases and position explicitly against the crowded anti-detect substrate, or the differentiation will read as overclaimed.

votes.reasoning:
The claim's narrow premise about the named *stealth benchmarks* holds: Paterson's anti-detect benchmark and Kynal's comparison test driver-level engines (nodriver/Patchright/Zendriver vs Cloudflare/DataDome), and browser-use/benchmark + Skyvern's Web Bench measure agent task success-rate (incl. under bot-detection), not framework-layer detectability. BUT the load-bearing assertion — that NO ONE evaluates the agentic-framework layer for the behavioral signals driver-stealth patches miss — is directly refuted by a primary source.

FP-Agent: Fingerprinting AI Browsing Agents (arXiv 2605.01247, May 2026; Vekaria/Shafiq et al., UC Davis) bills itself as "the first controlled measurement study of seven AI browsing agents and human users." It fingerprints exactly the agentic-framework layer — including Browser Use (v0.9.2) and Skyvern (v0.2.23), two of the four frameworks the claim names, plus five proprietary agents (Atlas, ChatGPT Agent, Claude for Chrome, Comet, Manus). Its central finding is precisely the gap the claim says is unaddressed: "browser fingerprints provide limited discriminative power when shared by multiple agents," whereas behavioral fingerprints (typing rhythm, scrolling, mouse trajectory) "separate AI browsing agents from humans and one another" — i.e., signals at a layer above driver/browser stealth patches. Its Cloudflare case study makes the point explicit: FP-Agent detects all 7 agents where Cloudflare (driver-level detection) detects only one.

Caveats (why this is refuted, not a slam-dunk on every word): (1) Coverage is partial — FP-Agent does not test Stagehand or Feather. (2) Signal taxonomy differs: FP-Agent's behavioral features are human-interaction-emulation signals (typing/mouse/scroll), NOT the specific "LLM pacing, DOM observation loops, tool-call cadence" the claim foregrounds. A genuinely novel niche may remain for LLM-decision-cadence / tool-call-timing signals specifically. But the claim asserts the *broad* category — agentic-framework-layer behavioral detectability beyond driver stealth — is something "none evaluate," and a published, code-and-data-available paper does exactly that comparative evaluation across the named frameworks. The competitor exists.
